items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “returning a degraded environment towards its original condition”.
items.answer: Restoration
items.markingKey: Restoration: returning a degraded environment towards its original condition. [1]

items.stem: Explain the strategies used to restore degraded rivers.
items.answer: Treatment of sewage and industrial effluent; discharge limits and monitoring; removal of contaminated sediment; re-naturalising channels and floodplains; fish passes; international cooperation on shared rivers.

items.stem: Explain how degraded land can be restored.
items.answer: Remediation of contaminated soils; capping landfill; replanting native vegetation; terracing and erosion control; reintroduction of species; reuse of brownfield sites.

items.stem: “Legislation is the most effective way to restore degraded environments.” Discuss. In your answer you may refer to stakeholders, regulation and technology.
items.answer: For: Laws and enforcement (Clean Air Act 1956, EU Water Framework Directive, polluter pays) forced industries to clean up and drove river and air recovery. Against: Funding, technology (treatment works), community involvement, market incentives and international cooperation are also needed; laws without enforcement fail (Ganga Action Plan). Conclusion: Legislation provides the framework, but restoration also needs funding, technology and cooperation.

items.stem: Explain the factors that influence the success of restoration.
items.answer: Funding; political will and legislation; enforcement; stakeholder cooperation; scale and severity of degradation; time; monitoring.

items.stem: Explain why conflicts arise in the management of degraded environments.
items.answer: Stakeholders have different priorities (profit, jobs, health, conservation); costs and benefits fall on different groups; uncertainty over causes; who pays; short-term vs long-term interests.

items.stem: Explain the role of NGOs in environmental management.
items.answer: Campaign and raise awareness; monitor pollution; take legal action; fund and run projects; represent local communities; but may lack power and funding.

items.stem: “Conflict between stakeholders is the main obstacle to managing degraded environments.” How far do you agree with this statement? In your answer you may refer to governance, funding and stakeholders.
items.answer: For: Opposition from industry, farmers and governments seeking growth delays action; disputes over cost-sharing on international rivers. Against: Lack of funding, technology, scientific understanding and enforcement capacity can be greater obstacles; some schemes succeed despite conflict through legislation. Conclusion: Conflict is a major obstacle, but funding and governance often determine whether it can be overcome.

items.stem: Explain why it is difficult to evaluate the success of managing a degraded environment.
items.answer: Success depends on the criteria chosen; long time scales; changes may be due to other factors (industrial decline, weather); limited monitoring data; different stakeholders judge success differently.

items.stem: Explain why the clean-up of the Ganges has been difficult.
items.answer: Huge population and untreated sewage from many cities; industrial effluent (tanneries at Kanpur); religious practices; weak enforcement; many states and agencies; low flows from abstraction.

items.stem: Using one named example of the management of a degraded environment, evaluate the success of the management.
items.answer: the River Thames, London: From biologically dead in 1957 to about 125 fish species, seals and seahorses; but sewage overflows still occurred in heavy rain, microplastics and road run-off remain, and costs fall on water bills.

items.stem: Using a named example of the management of a degraded environment you have studied, evaluate the extent to which the management has been successful.
items.answer: Model answer (the River Ganges, India (Ganga Action Plan and Namami Gange)): Ganga Action Plan (1986), then Namami Gange (2014, about US$3 billion): sewage treatment plants, closure or treatment of tannery effluent, riverfront development, crematoria improvements, river surface cleaning, afforestation. items.stem: “The management of degraded environments is more successful in HICs than in LICs and NICs.” How far do you agree with this statement? In your answer you may refer to funding and regulation.

items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 4 marks for accurate, place-specific points (names, dates, figures), max 2 if general. Named strategies, organisations, dates and costs. [5]

items.stem: Briefly evaluate the success of the management, for the River Thames, London or another example of the management of a degraded environment.
items.answer: the River Thames, London: From biologically dead in 1957 to about 125 fish species, seals and seahorses; but sewage overflows still occurred in heavy rain, microplastics and road run-off remain, and costs fall on water bills.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 4 marks for accurate, place-specific points (names, dates, figures), max 2 if general. Measured outcomes against criteria; continuing problems. [5]

items.stem: “The management of degraded environments is more successful in HICs than in LICs and NICs.” How far do you agree with this statement? In your answer you may refer to regulation and funding.
items.answer: For: HICs have funding, technology, strong regulation and monitoring: Thames and Rhine recoveries. Against: Mexico City and Beijing have reduced pollution substantially; HICs still have problems (Thames overflows); LICs often face larger populations and faster growth rather than lower competence. Conclusion: Resources and governance favour HICs, but NICs show that strong policy can bring major improvements.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain how degraded land can be restored. (b) A revision website states: “International cooperation is needed to restore shared rivers.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Remediation of contaminated soils; capping landfill; replanting native vegetation; terracing and erosion control; reintroduction of species; reuse of brownfield sites. (b) Correct. Pollution from upstream countries affects those downstream.
items.markingKey: (a) [3] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain how degraded land can be restored. (b) Explain the factors that influence the success of restoration.
items.answer: (a) Remediation of contaminated soils; capping landfill; replanting native vegetation; terracing and erosion control; reintroduction of species; reuse of brownfield sites. (b) Funding; political will and legislation; enforcement; stakeholder cooperation; scale and severity of degradation; time; monitoring.

items.stem: Tomás argues that legislation is the most effective way to restore degraded environments. How far do you agree? Support your answer with examples. In your answer you may refer to stakeholders and regulation.
items.answer: For: Laws and enforcement (Clean Air Act 1956, EU Water Framework Directive, polluter pays) forced industries to clean up and drove river and air recovery. Against: Funding, technology (treatment works), community involvement, market incentives and international cooperation are also needed; laws without enforcement fail (Ganga Action Plan). Conclusion: Legislation provides the framework, but restoration also needs funding, technology and cooperation.

items.stem: A revision website states: “Conflicts between stakeholders can never be resolved.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Negotiation, compensation and participatory planning can resolve many conflicts.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain the role of NGOs in environmental management. (b) Explain why conflicts arise in the management of degraded environments.
items.answer: (a) Campaign and raise awareness; monitor pollution; take legal action; fund and run projects; represent local communities; but may lack power and funding. (b) Stakeholders have different priorities (profit, jobs, health, conservation); costs and benefits fall on different groups; uncertainty over causes; who pays; short-term vs long-term interests.

items.stem: Table 22.2 is a conflict matrix for stakeholders in a scheme to clean up a polluted river. Pairs: factory owners / local fishers: conflict; factory owners / water company: conflict; factory owners / conservation NGO: conflict; factory owners / city council: compatible; local fishers / water company: conflict; local fishers / conservation NGO: compatible; local fishers / city council: neutral; water company / conservation NGO: neutral; water company / city council: neutral; conservation NGO / city council: neutral. Calculate the number and percentage of stakeholder pairs that are in conflict.
items.answer: 4 of 10 pairs = 40%

items.stem: Table 22.2 is a conflict matrix for stakeholders in a scheme to clean up a polluted river. Pairs: factory owners / local fishers: conflict; factory owners / water company: conflict; factory owners / conservation NGO: conflict; factory owners / city council: conflict; local fishers / water company: neutral; local fishers / conservation NGO: conflict; local fishers / city council: compatible; water company / conservation NGO: conflict; water company / city council: neutral; conservation NGO / city council: compatible. (a) Calculate the number and percentage of stakeholder pairs that are in conflict. (b) Identify the stakeholder involved in the most conflicts and suggest why.
items.answer: (a) 6 of 10 pairs = 60% (b) Factory owners (4 conflicts): cleaning up would require costly treatment of its effluent, while the others gain from cleaner water.

items.stem: “Conflict between stakeholders is the main obstacle to managing degraded environments.” Discuss.
items.answer: For: Opposition from industry, farmers and governments seeking growth delays action; disputes over cost-sharing on international rivers. Against: Lack of funding, technology, scientific understanding and enforcement capacity can be greater obstacles; some schemes succeed despite conflict through legislation. Conclusion: Conflict is a major obstacle, but funding and governance often determine whether it can be overcome.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “Hoy No Circula”?
options: Measurable indicators, such as pollutant levels or species numbers, used to judge whether management has worked.
A point where sewage and rainwater overflow into a river when sewers are full.
A 25 km “super sewer” under London, completed in the mid-2020s, to stop sewage overflows into the Thames.
A Mexico City scheme (1989) banning cars from driving on one weekday according to their number plate.
items.answer: A Mexico City scheme (1989) banning cars from driving on one weekday according to their number plate.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A student writes: “The Thames now supports over 100 species of fish.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain why the clean-up of the Ganges has been difficult.
items.answer: (a) Correct. About 125 species have been recorded since the clean-up. (b) Huge population and untreated sewage from many cities; industrial effluent (tanneries at Kanpur); religious practices; weak enforcement; many states and agencies; low flows from abstraction.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) [3]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) In a class discussion, a student says: “Mexico City’s air quality has not changed since 1990.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) A student writes: “The Thames now supports over 100 species of fish.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. Lead, sulphur dioxide and carbon monoxide fell sharply, though ozone and PM2.5 remain problems. (b) Correct. About 125 species have been recorded since the clean-up.

items.answer: the River Thames, London: From the 1960s new sewage treatment works (Beckton, Crossness) and controls on industrial discharges; Thames Water and the Environment Agency monitoring; Thames Tideway Tunnel (about £4.5 billion) to capture combined sewer overflows.

items.stem: Referring to the River Ganges, India (Ganga Action Plan and Namami Gange) or another example of the management of a degraded environment, describe the strategies used to manage the degraded environment. To what extent is your chosen example typical of the management of a degraded environment?
items.answer: Model answer (the River Ganges, India (Ganga Action Plan and Namami Gange)): Ganga Action Plan (1986), then Namami Gange (2014, about US$3 billion): sewage treatment plants, closure or treatment of tannery effluent, riverfront development, crematoria improvements, river surface cleaning, afforestation. Treatment capacity has increased and dissolved oxygen improved at some sites; but faecal coliforms remain far above bathing standards in many places, plants operate below capacity, and enforcement and coordination are weak.
